summary: Defines the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER) for ASN.1, a human-readable text encoding for values of any ASN.1 data type. This makes it easier to display and write values than with the binary encodings commonly used. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER) give ASN.1 values a readable UTF-8 text form. GSER can help people inspect or exchange values, but it cannot always reproduce the exact original binary encoding.

questions: how are asn.1 values written as text
subtitle: A human-readable UTF-8 encoding for values of ASN.1 data types.

tldr.problem: ASN.1 values are commonly exchanged in encodings that are difficult for people to read, while directory data benefits from a readable text form.
tldr.mechanism: GSER defines a UTF-8 text representation for values of ASN.1 types, with rules for strings, numbers, choices, sequences, and other types.
tldr.outcome: GSER is not canonical and cannot always reproduce the original binary encoding. RFC 3641 is updated by RFC 4792.

today: RFC 3641 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2003 and is updated by RFC 4792.

sections.title: A Readable Form for ASN.1 Values
sections.content:
GSER defines a human-readable UTF-8 encoding for values of any ASN.1 type. An ASN.1 value is an abstract value independent of its encoding; BER is one encoding, and GSER is another.

The rules are based on ASN.1 value notation and are intended primarily for LDAP attribute and assertion syntaxes. Other specifications can use GSER where a readable rendering of ASN.1 values is useful.
sections.plainLanguage: GSER represents an ASN.1 value as readable UTF-8 text instead of a binary encoding. It is especially intended for readable directory data.

sections.title: Text Strings and Identifiers
sections.content:
Restricted character strings are written as UTF-8 characters between double quotes, with an embedded double quote written twice. GeneralizedTime, UTCTime, and ObjectDescriptor values use the same quoted-string form.

ASN.1 identifiers begin with a lowercase letter and continue with letters, digits, or hyphens under the identifier rules. Tags and constraints do not appear in the GSER text representation.
sections.plainLanguage: String values use quotation marks, and a quotation mark inside the value is doubled. Type tags and constraints are not written into the text.

sections.title: Simple Values
sections.content:
GSER writes BOOLEAN values as TRUE or FALSE, NULL as NULL, and INTEGER values as decimal numbers or named identifiers. ENUMERATED values use their defined identifiers.

BIT STRING values can use binary digits, hexadecimal digits, or a list of named bits. OCTET STRING values use pairs of hexadecimal digits between single quotes followed by H. Object identifiers use dotted decimal or a descriptor name.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic values have direct text forms: words for true or false, decimal digits for integers, and hexadecimal pairs for bytes. The ASN.1 type determines which form is valid.

sections.title: Choices, Sequences, and Sets
sections.content:
A CHOICE normally uses the chosen alternative's identifier, a colon, and its value. A SEQUENCE or SET uses braces around named components in the order of the type definition. SEQUENCE OF and SET OF use braces around the list of values.

Because types may gain components, an implementation should be able to skip a named value whose identifier it does not recognize. A specification may declare a CHOICE between string types to be a ChoiceOfStrings type, allowing a plain string form.
sections.plainLanguage: Composite values use braces and labels to show their parts. An implementation should be able to skip a component label it does not recognize when a type has been extended.

sections.title: Special Forms and Transfer Identification
sections.content:
Some named ASN.1 types have special string encodings. Distinguished names use the LDAP string form, and ORAddress uses its defined textual representation; each is then quoted using the appropriate string form.

The RFC assigns the object identifier { 1 2 36 79672281 0 0 } to identify GSER as a transfer syntax. It can identify a GSER-encoded value carried inside an EMBEDDED PDV.
sections.plainLanguage: Some complex values keep an established text representation instead of using the general GSER rules. An object identifier can name GSER when a transfer syntax must be identified.

sections.title: Why GSER Is Not for Signatures
sections.content:
GSER does not define a canonical encoding. Converting a GSER value to another encoding and back may not reproduce the same text bytes. Some ASN.1 string values also cannot be converted back to the exact original octets.

GSER must not be used when a canonical encoding or exact recovery of the original binary representation is required, such as for digital signature verification. Security-sensitive comparisons must use the underlying abstract value, regardless of its encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Two valid GSER texts for a value may not have identical bytes. Use a canonical encoding when signatures or exact recovery depend on matching bytes.
